evidence: OrderService.place: builds OrderLine/Order domain objects, calls product.reserve(quantity), and saves through the OrderRepository/ProductRepository interfaces, which is use-case coordination
OrderService.advance/cancel: hand state changes to order.advanceTo(state), order.cancel() and product.release(), so the domain rules stay in domain objects
OrderService.toDto: maps the domain Order to the application OrderDto, which belongs in the application layer
There is no SQL, HTTP, file I/O or framework code in src/application/order-service.ts
place(): the `product.stock < quantity` pre-check happens before any change, which looks like an all-or-nothing check rather than domain logic that belongs elsewhere
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/application/order-service.ts does what an application-layer use-case service should do. It turns input DTOs into domain objects and loads and saves aggregates through domain repository interfaces. It hands state changes to domain methods (Order.advanceTo, Order.cancel, Product.reserve, Product.release), coordinates work across the Order and Product aggregates, and maps results back to DTOs. It has no persistence, transport or framework code. In place(), the check `product.stock < quantity` runs before any reservation is made. That looks like a pre-check so the multi-product operation either fully succeeds or makes no change, not a domain rule taken out of the domain layer: the rule itself still lives in Product.reserve. The duplicate-order check and the missing-entity errors are normal application-level coordination. The default ID generator (crypto.randomUUID) is an injectable collaborator, not infrastructure logic. The stock pre-check could be read as a borderline business rule, so confidence is moderate.
